item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q010_rossmann_family_function_divergence","answer":"SCOPe places these domains in the alpha/beta class (c), NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold (c.2), NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold superfamily (c.2.1), and specifically the alcohol-dehydrogenase-like C-terminal-domain family (c.2.1.1). CoA-binding domains and potassium-channel NAD-binding domains are functionally divergent protein-level groups within that family. Thus SCOPe supports a relatively strong domain-level evolutionary relationship—stronger than merely sharing a Rossmann fold—but does not classify them as functionally interchangeable. “Alcohol-dehydrogenase-like” describes the structural/evolutionary family, not a guaranteed alcohol-dehydrogenase activity: the CoA-binding member may bind CoA, whereas the potassium-channel member is an NAD-binding regulatory domain associated with a channel rather than necessarily an enzyme. Homology applies only to the classified domain, not automatically to the full multidomain proteins. Function, substrate, catalytic residues, oligomeric state, and channel regulation must not be transferred solely from this classification; they require sequence/profile and residue analysis plus ligand-binding, biochemical, or electrophysiological evidence. A structure from another subgroup can guide modeling of the conserved Rossmann-like core, but same-function and same-ligand-state templates are preferable for variable loops, binding sites, interfaces, and representative selection.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
